meta.title: Old English Alphabet and Pronunciation
meta.subtitle: 42 letters and spellings · 8 reading rules
meta.desc: How to read Old English: 42 letters and spellings and 8 reading rules, the first deck of the Old English collection. A letter is two cards — see it and recall its sound, see the sound and recall the letter, each with its own schedule — and a reading rule is one. The vowels short and long, the diphthongs (ea, eo, ie), the consonants that are not said as in modern English (ċ, ġ, sċ, ċġ, h after a vowel, f s and þ between voiced sounds), what holds for every word (no letter is silent, a double consonant is long, ġe- is never stressed), the letters said as today, and the scribes' own letters: wynn (ƿ), the insular g, ꝥ for þæt and ⁊ for and. The reading rules are what a text prints differently from a card: no macron and no dot, ð for þ, y for ie, an acute in Thorpe's Ælfric — and how to read the line of IPA under every headword of the level decks, which is the only sound there is, since no voice reads Old English. Sources. Every IPA symbol and every English comparison is a row of Wikipedia's key, Help:IPA/Old English (revision 1355663743); every rule is quoted from that key's notes, from 'Old English phonology' (revision 1364038675) or from the Orthography section of 'Old English' (revision 1388030632), CC BY-SA 4.0, and the quotation is on the card. The sounds are a scholarly reconstruction: the key itself says the nature of r is unknown and that ie is disputed. The example words are cards of Old English Level 1 with that deck's own pronunciation and meaning (English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction, CC BY-SA 4.0). THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). What these cards are for, counted on Old English Level 1: of its 500 headwords 244 carry a macron, 52 a dotted ċ and 87 a dotted ġ; 66 have an f, s or þ between voiced sounds; 87 are not stressed on their first syllable (51 begin with ġe-); 291 give their pronunciation between slashes, 201 between square brackets and 8 not at all. Of the 728 sentences from Thorpe's Ælfric on those cards none prints a macron or a dot, 598 print ð and 332 an acute; 27 of Tatoeba's 315 print ƿ. THE PACE: at the default of ten new cards a day — a letter is two cards, a reading rule one — this deck is 92 cards, days 1 to 10, and Level 1 follows from day 10 to day 110.

fields.Name: short a
fields.Sound: [ɑ] cot (American English)
fields.Example: habban[ˈhɑb.bɑn]to have, possess

fields.Name: long a
fields.Sound: [ɑː] father

fields.Name: ash (æsc)
fields.Sound: [æ] cat “⟨æ⟩ (æsc, modern ash)”

fields.Name: long ash
fields.Sound: [æː] dad

fields.Name: short e
fields.Sound: [e] Spanish te

fields.Name: long e
fields.Sound: [eː] similar to made

fields.Name: short i
fields.Sound: [i] feet

fields.Name: long i
fields.Sound: [iː] need

fields.Name: short o
fields.Sound: [o] short

fields.Name: long o
fields.Sound: [oː] door

fields.Name: short u
fields.Sound: [u] pull
fields.Example: sunu/ˈsu.nu/son, male child

fields.Name: long u
fields.Sound: [uː] pool

fields.Name: short y
fields.Sound: [y] youth (some dialects); French tu

fields.Name: long y
fields.Sound: [yː] you (some dialects); German Dürer

fields.Ask: The line over the vowel: what does it mean, and who wrote it?
fields.Rule: A long vowel. The line, a macron, is a modern editor's: the manuscripts mark no length, so a text may print the same word without it.
fields.Quote: “Macrons are used to indicate long vowels, where usually no distinction was made between long and short vowels in the originals.”

fields.Ask: Slashes or square brackets under a headword: what is the difference?
fields.Rule: Square brackets give the sounds as they are said, slashes only the sounds the word is built from: an f, s or þ said [v], [z], [ð] is still /f/, /s/, /θ/ between slashes. ː marks a long sound and ˈ stands before the stressed syllable. These cards join the two vowels of a diphthong with a tie and put the length mark after both: [æ͜ɑː].
fields.Quote:
“the phoneme /θ/ was pronounced as the voiced sound [ð] in the words eorðe 'earth' and fæþm 'fathom', which can be phonemically transcibed as /ˈe͝orθe/, /ˈfæθm/ and phonetically transcribed as [ˈe͝orðe], [ˈfæðm].”
“Long monophthongs are marked by placing the length symbol ⟨ː⟩ after the vowel symbol”
“stress mark (placed right before the stressed syllable)”
fields.Source: Wikipedia, "Help:IPA/Old English", revision 1355663743; Wikipedia, "Old English phonology", revision 1364038675

fields.Name: short diphthong
fields.Sound: [æɑ] mouth (Cockney)

fields.Name: long diphthong
fields.Sound: [æːɑ] now (Cockney)

fields.Name: short diphthong
fields.Sound: [eo] bed + rod

fields.Name: long diphthong
fields.Sound: [eːo] snail (MLE)
fields.Example: dēofol[ˈde͜oː.vol]a demon, devil

fields.Name: short diphthong (early West Saxon)
fields.Sound: [iy] feet + French tu “The diphthongs ⟨ie īe⟩ occurred in West Saxon and may have been pronounced /ie iːe/ or /iy iːy/.”

fields.Name: long diphthong (early West Saxon)
fields.Sound: [iːy] need + French tu “The diphthongs ⟨ie īe⟩ occurred in West Saxon and may have been pronounced /ie iːe/ or /iy iːy/.”

fields.Ask: One word, three spellings. Which is the early one, and what do later texts write?
fields.Rule: ie is early West Saxon, and the spelling the cards print. Late West Saxon writes y for it, or i: a word under ie on its card can stand under y in a sentence.
fields.Quote:
“The diphthong ⟨ie⟩ ie, īe was found exclusively in Early West Saxon.”
“This "unstable ī̆" sound typically corresponds to ȳ̆ in Late West Saxon, as in gelȳfan for earlier gelīefan and gelīfan ('to believe').”

fields.Name: c without a dot
fields.Sound: [k] king “Word-initially before another consonant, the pronunciation of ⟨c⟩ is always /k/; before ⟨i⟩, it is usually /tʃ/.”
fields.Example:
cuman/ˈku.mɑn/to come
cyning[ˈky.niŋɡ]king

fields.Name: c with a dot
fields.Sound: [tʃ] cheese “⟨ċ ċġ sċ⟩, with a dot above, represent postalveolar [tʃ dʒ ʃ] in modern editions; ⟨ġ⟩ usually represents the palatal approximant [j] but represents [dʒ] after ⟨n⟩.”
fields.Example:
ċild[t͡ʃiɫd]child
iċ/it͡ʃ/I

fields.Name: g without a dot
fields.Sound: [ɡ] good, the key's example gōd; [ɣ] Spanish fuego, its examples magan and dagum
fields.Example:
gōd/ɡoːd/good
āstīgan[ɑːˈstiː.ɣɑn]to go, proceed

fields.Name: g with a dot
fields.Sound: [j] year; after n, [dʒ] jam “⟨ċ ċġ sċ⟩, with a dot above, represent postalveolar [tʃ dʒ ʃ] in modern editions; ⟨ġ⟩ usually represents the palatal approximant [j] but represents [dʒ] after ⟨n⟩.”
fields.Example:
ġēar/jæ͜ɑːr/year
dæġ/dæj/day,

fields.Name: cg
fields.Sound: [dʒ] jam, doubled between vowels: [ddʒ] “in modern editions, the palatal geminate is sometimes written ⟨ċġ⟩ to distinguish it from velar ⟨cg⟩.”
fields.Example: seċġan[ˈsed.d͡ʒɑn]to say, tell

fields.Name: sc
fields.Sound: [ʃ] shadow “At the start of a word, the usual pronunciation is palatalised sċ /ʃ/.”
fields.Example:
sċulan/ˈʃu.lɑn/should
sċēap/ʃæ͜ɑːp/sheep

fields.Name: h
fields.Sound: [h] heaven at the start of a word; [ç] hue after a front vowel; otherwise [x] loch (Scottish English) “it was pronounced [h] word-initially, [ç] when it was single and after a front vowel, and [x] otherwise.”
fields.Example:
hund[hund]dog
niht[niçt]night

fields.Name: h before a consonant
fields.Sound: [ʍ] what (some speakers); [l̥] whispered leaf; [n̥] whispered near; [r̥] whispered read “The sonorants /r l n w/ had voiceless versions [l̥ r̥ n̥ ʍ], which developed from the earlier consonant clusters /xl xr xn xw/.”
fields.Example:
hwæt[ʍæt]what
hlāf[l̥ɑːf]bread

fields.Name: f
fields.Sound: [f] father; single between voiced sounds, [v] over “⟨s f ð/þ⟩ represented voiceless fricatives [s f θ] at the beginning and the end of a word or when doubled in the middle but represented voiced fricatives [z v ð] when single between voiced sounds.”
fields.Example:
fæder/ˈfæ.der/father
heofon[ˈhe͜o.von]sky

fields.Name: s
fields.Sound: [s] sun; single between voiced sounds, [z] busy “⟨s f ð/þ⟩ represented voiceless fricatives [s f θ] at the beginning and the end of a word or when doubled in the middle but represented voiced fricatives [z v ð] when single between voiced sounds.”
fields.Example:
sāwol/ˈsɑː.wol/soul
ārīsan[ɑːˈriː.zɑn]to rise, arise, get up

fields.Name: thorn and eth
fields.Sound: [θ] through; single between voiced sounds, [ð] other. Two letters, one sound “Both ⟨þ⟩ and ⟨ð⟩ could represent either allophone of /θ/, voiceless [θ] or voiced [ð], but some texts show a tendency to use ⟨þ⟩ at the start of words and ⟨ð⟩ in the middle or at the end of a word.”
fields.Example:
þing[θiŋɡ]thing
ōþer[ˈoː.ðer]other

fields.Name: r
fields.Sound: [r] read; before a consonant [rˠ] ruff “The exact nature of the rhotic /r/ is unknown.”
fields.Example:
rīċe/ˈriː.t͡ʃe/kingdom, empire
heorte[ˈhe͜orˠ.te]heart

fields.Name: x
fields.Sound: [ks]: [k] king and [s] sun “⟨x⟩ represented the cluster /ks/, as Modern English still does.”

fields.Name: n before g
fields.Sound: [ŋɡ]: [ŋ] young, then [ɡ] good “The allophone [ŋ] occurred before a velar plosive ([k] or [ɡ]).”
fields.Example:
singan[ˈsiŋ.ɡɑn]to sing, chant
cyning[ˈky.niŋɡ]king

fields.Ask: c or ċ, g or ġ: who writes the dot?
fields.Rule: A modern editor, to tell the palatal sounds from the velar ones. The manuscripts print plain c and g, and so do the sentences here from Thorpe's Ælfric: the card's headword shows which it is.
fields.Quote: “modern editions often distinguish between velar and palatal ⟨c⟩ and ⟨g⟩ by placing dots above the palatals: ⟨ċ⟩, ⟨ġ⟩.”

fields.Rule: No: one sound, two letters, and a scribe writes either. The cards print þ; a sentence may print ð in the same word.
fields.Quote: “Both ⟨þ⟩ and ⟨ð⟩ could represent either allophone of /θ/, voiceless [θ] or voiced [ð], but some texts show a tendency to use ⟨þ⟩ at the start of words and ⟨ð⟩ in the middle or at the end of a word.”

fields.Ask: How are f, s and þ said between two voiced sounds?
fields.Rule: Voiced, when single: [v], [z], [ð]. At the beginning or the end of a word, or doubled, they are [f], [s], [θ].
fields.Quote: “⟨s f ð/þ⟩ represented voiceless fricatives [s f θ] at the beginning and the end of a word or when doubled in the middle but represented voiced fricatives [z v ð] when single between voiced sounds.”

fields.Name: two consonants at the start
fields.Sound: both are said: no letter is silent “There were not usually any silent letters – in the word cniht, for example, both the ⟨c⟩ and ⟨h⟩ were pronounced”
fields.Example:
cniht[kniçt]boy
āwrītanto write, write out, write down, compose

fields.Name: double consonants
fields.Sound: a double consonant is said longer than a single one “Old English had geminate (double) consonants, which were pronounced longer than single consonants.”
fields.Example:
habban[ˈhɑb.bɑn]to have, possess
sittan/ˈsit.tɑn/to sit

fields.Name: an unstressed prefix
fields.Sound: [je], [j] year and [e] Spanish te: never stressed, and no more are be- and, nearly always, for- “The prefixes ġe- and be- were always fully unstressed, and the prefix for- was nearly always unstressed.”
fields.Example:
ġesēon/jeˈse͜oːn/to see
forġiefan[forˈji͜y.vɑn]to give

fields.Rule: On the first syllable of the root: the first syllable of the word, unless the word begins with an unstressed prefix — ġe- and be- always, for- nearly always.
fields.Quote:
“Stress typically could be found only on the first or leftmost syllable of a root morpheme.”
“The prefixes ġe- and be- were always fully unstressed, and the prefix for- was nearly always unstressed.”

fields.Letter: b, d, l, m, n, p, t, w
fields.Name: the rest
fields.Sound: [b] busy, [d] do, [l] leaf, [m] mother, [n] near, [p] path, [t] stand, [w] wife
fields.Example:
mōdor/ˈmoː.dor/mother
wīf/wiːf/woman
fields.Word: b, d, l, m, n, p, t, w

fields.Name: wynn
fields.Sound: the manuscripts' letter for [w] wife; editions print w, and some of Tatoeba's sentences print ƿ “Old English manuscripts typically represented the sound /w/ with the letter ⟨ƿ⟩, called wynn and derived from the rune of the same name.” “The letter ⟨w⟩ did not exist in the Early Middle Ages, when Old English was spoken.”

fields.Name: insular g
fields.Sound: the manuscripts' shape of g, read as g or ġ; editions print g “In Old English manuscripts, this letter usually took its insular form ⟨ᵹ⟩.”

fields.Name: the abbreviation for þæt
fields.Sound: a thorn with a stroke: the scribes' shorthand for þæt “A common scribal abbreviation was a thorn with a stroke ⟨ꝥ⟩, which was used for the pronoun þæt (that).”

fields.Name: the abbreviation for and
fields.Sound: the scribes' sign for and, shaped like a 7 “Also used was the Tironian note ⟨⁊⟩ (a character similar to the digit ⟨7⟩) for the conjunction and.”

fields.Ask: A mark the cards never print. What is it?
fields.Rule: Not another vowel. Thorpe's 1844 text of Ælfric prints an acute over some vowels and never a macron; older editions used the acute. Read the word as its card spells it.
fields.Quote: “In some older editions an acute accent mark was used for consistency with Old Norse conventions.”
